questions.q: State the definition of an equivalence relation on a set A. What three properties must it satisfy?
questions.a: An equivalence relation on a set A is a relation R ⊆ A × A that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R ∀ a ∈ A. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R ∀ a, b ∈ A. Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R ∀ a, b, c ∈ A. A wrong answer (e.g., missing one property or confusing symmetric with transitive) reveals the student has not internalized the precise logical structure — they may think "equivalence" means only "symmetric" or only "reflexive and symmetric", which is a common error that leads to incomplete verifications in board exams.

questions.q: Consider the relation R on the set of integers Z defined by (a, b) ∈ R iff a − b is a multiple of 3. Is R an equivalence relation? Explain why or why not by checking each property.
questions.a: Yes, R is an equivalence relation. Reflexive: a − a = 0 = 3·0, so (a, a) ∈ R. Symmetric: if a − b = 3k, then b − a = −3k = 3(−k), so (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: if a − b = 3k and b − c = 3m, then a − c = (a − b) + (b − c) = 3(k + m), so (a, c) ∈ R. A student who says "yes" but cannot show the algebraic step for transitivity (e.g., just says "it's transitive because multiples of 3 add up") reveals a gap in writing rigorous proofs — board exams require explicit demonstration that a − c is a multiple of 3 using the given expressions.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Define R = {(a, b) ∈ A × A : |a − b| is even}. Determine whether R is an equivalence relation. If yes, find the equivalence class [1] and [2].
questions.a: R is an equivalence relation. Reflexive: |a − a| = 0 (even) ⇒ (a, a) ∈ R. Symmetric: |a − b| = |b − a|, so if |a − b| is even then |b − a| is even. Transitive: if |a − b| and |b − c| are even, then a − b and b − c are even ⇒ (a − b) + (b − c) = a − c is even ⇒ |a − c| is even. Equivalence classes: [1] = {1, 3, 5} (all odd numbers), [2] = {2, 4, 6} (all even numbers). A wrong answer where a student claims [1] = {1, 2} or includes 2 in [1] reveals they are not using the definition |a − b| even correctly — they may be confusing "even difference" with "both even" or "both odd" without checking the actual condition.

questions.q: Let R₁ and R₂ be two equivalence relations on the same set A. Is R₁ ∪ R₂ necessarily an equivalence relation? Is R₁ ∩ R₂ necessarily an equivalence relation? Justify your answers.
questions.a: R₁ ∩ R₂ is always an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive properties are preserved under intersection). R₁ ∪ R₂ is NOT necessarily an equivalence relation — it is reflexive and symmetric, but may fail transitivity. Counterexample: A = {1, 2, 3}, R₁ = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}, R₂ = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(2,3),(3,2)}. Then (1,2) ∈ R₁ ∪ R₂ and (2,3) ∈ R₁ ∪ R₂ but (1,3) ∉ R₁ ∪ R₂. A student who claims both are equivalence relations reveals a misunderstanding of how transitivity behaves under union — they may assume properties are preserved under all set operations, which is a classic competitive exam trap.

questions.q: A student writes: "The relation R = {(1,2), (2,1)} on the set {1,2,3} is symmetric and transitive, so it must be reflexive by the following argument: since (1,2) and (2,1) are in R, by transitivity (1,1) must be in R. Similarly (2,2) ∈ R. And (3,3) is automatically in R because...?" Identify the flaw in this reasoning.
questions.a: The flaw is that transitivity only gives (1,1) and (2,2) because we have pairs involving 1 and 2. There is NO pair involving 3 in R, so we cannot deduce (3,3) ∈ R from symmetry and transitivity alone. Reflexivity requires (a,a) ∈ R for EVERY a ∈ A, including 3. The student's argument incorrectly assumes that symmetry and transitivity imply reflexivity on the whole set — they only imply reflexivity on the subset of elements that appear in some pair of R. This is a well-known fallacy: a symmetric and transitive relation is reflexive only on its domain of definition, not necessarily on the whole set A.

questions.q: Construct an equivalence relation on the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} that has exactly three equivalence classes, with class sizes 1, 2, and 3. Write the relation explicitly as a set of ordered pairs.
questions.a: One possible partition: {1}, {2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}. The equivalence relation R consists of all pairs within each class: R = {(1,1), (2,2),(2,3),(3,2),(3,3), (4,4),(4,5),(4,6),(5,4),(5,5),(5,6),(6,4),(6,5),(6,6)}. Check: reflexive (all (a,a) present), symmetric (if (a,b) in R then (b,a) in R), transitive (within each class, all pairs are present). A student who produces a relation missing some pairs (e.g., missing (4,6) or (5,4)) reveals they do not understand that an equivalence class must contain ALL pairs between its elements — they may think only adjacent elements are related, confusing equivalence with a partial order or a graph.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: An equivalence relation on a set A is a relation R ⊆ A × A that satisfies three properties ______: (1) Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A; (2) Symmetric: if (a, b) ∈ R then (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b ∈ A; (3) Transitive: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R then (a, c) ∈ R for all a, b, c ∈ A.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the class monitor and need to group all 40 students of Class XII into teams such that every student is in exactly one team and students in the same team share a specific ______ — say, the same birth month.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the class monitor and need to group all ______ students of Class XII into teams such that every student is in exactly one team and students in the same team share a specific property — say, the same birth month.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) verify whether a given relation is an equivalence relation by checking all three properties with rigorous justification, (2) determine the equivalence classes of a given equivalence relation and show they form a partition of the set, and (3) construct an equivalence relation from a given partition of a set.
